opus-5.5.text:
Edge is something we think about a lot, but I want to be honest about how we sequence it. Our focus right now is the data center, because that's where the inference problem is most acute. You have these large models being served to millions of users, and the economics of memory bandwidth, latency and power just don't work with traditional architectures. That's the problem we built d-Matrix to solve, and we want to win there first.

That said, one of the reasons we went with a chiplet-based architecture from day one is that it gives us flexibility. The building blocks are modular. In the data center you might put a lot of chiplets together on a card and scale out across many cards to serve a big model. But the same core technology, our digital in-memory compute approach, where we bring compute right next to the memory to cut down on data movement, is fundamentally about efficiency. Efficiency matters even more at the edge, where you're power-constrained, thermally constrained and cost-constrained.

So the way I think about it is that edge isn't one market. There's what I'd call the near edge: on-prem servers, enterprise closets, telco infrastructure, maybe automotive and industrial systems that need serious inference capability but can't send everything back to a hyperscaler. That's a natural extension for us, because you can scale down the number of chiplets and still get the latency and efficiency benefits. Then there's the far edge, phones and tiny embedded devices, which is a very different business with different volume dynamics and incumbents. I'm not sure that's where we'd play directly, at least not in the near term.

The other trend that makes this interesting is that models are getting more efficient. You're seeing smaller, distilled models that are really capable, and a lot of agentic and real-time applications where latency is everything. As that happens, more inference will move closer to the user, and the architectures that do well will be the ones that solve the memory bottleneck without burning a ton of power. That plays to our strengths.

So the short answer is: data center first, because that's where the pain is today, but the platform was designed so we can take it to the edge when the market is ready, and I think that moment is coming faster than people expect.

r001.rationale: It says the chiplet building blocks are modular and that near-edge systems can use a scaled-down number of chiplets.

r002.rationale: It does not state that the software remains unchanged when the chiplet count changes.

r003.rationale: It describes edge as multiple markets and lists verticals, but does not identify differences in software stacks as a source of fragmentation.

r004.rationale: It says d-Matrix is prioritizing the data center because the inference problem is acute, but does not attribute deferring edge to limited organizational capacity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question we get a lot, and I want to be honest about where our head is at. d-Matrix was built from day one around a very specific problem, which is inference in the data center. Generative AI, transformer models, the economics of serving those models at scale. That's where the pain is most acute, and that's where our in-memory compute architecture gives you the biggest step up in performance per dollar and performance per watt. So the data center is the beachhead, and we're not distracted from that.

That said, the reason we built this as a chiplet platform rather than a monolithic chip is precisely because it gives us options. Chiplets let you compose. You can take the same core compute building block and pair it with different amounts of memory, different I/O, different packaging, and end up with products at very different power envelopes. So when people ask about the edge, I'd say the architecture is naturally suited to it. We don't have to go back to the drawing board.

But I'd also push back a little on what "edge" means. People hear edge and they think phones or cars. For us, the interesting edge is more like the enterprise edge, the telco edge, places where you have a rack or a few servers close to where data is generated and you want to run inference locally for latency, privacy, or cost reasons. That's a much shorter hop from where we are today than putting something in a handset.

So the way I think about it is in stages. Win in the data center first, prove the architecture with real customers. Then follow the workloads as they move outward, using the modularity of the chiplet approach to scale down into those edge deployments. And frankly, the market will tell us when. If the big consumer of inference compute stays in the cloud, we stay focused there. If it fragments outward, we're in a good position to follow it without having to reinvent ourselves.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether the software remains unchanged as the chiplet count changes.

r003.rationale: It mentions workloads potentially fragmenting outward, but does not identify differences in software stacks across edge verticals as a cause of fragmentation.

r004.rationale: It says d-Matrix will focus on the data center first, but does not attribute deferring edge expansion to limited organizational capacity to pursue both markets.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between taking the architecture to the edge and taking a data-center product and putting it at the edge. Those are different things. At the edge, power, cost, and the amount of memory you can support become much tighter constraints.

A chiplet approach gives you flexibility in how you assemble a solution. You can think about scaling the compute and memory to fit a particular workload, rather than building one large chip for every application. But you still have to start with the use case: What model needs to run? What latency does it require? What’s the power budget?

So I’d think about edge computing as a potential extension of the platform, with products designed around those requirements. The architecture gives you a starting point; it doesn’t eliminate the work of building the right product for that market.

sol-6.1.text: The way I think about it is that edge computing has a different set of constraints. You’re still trying to deliver efficient inference, but power, cost, and latency become very specific to the application. So the opportunity with a chiplet platform is to take a common architectural foundation and configure it for different requirements, rather than design a completely new chip every time. But you have to start with the workload. What model needs to run locally? How much memory does it need? What’s the power budget? Those answers should drive how you extend the platform.
